ordered_steps: State the complement in one sentence: product_of_inertia_area COMPUTES the product of inertia; this skill INTERPRETS its sign, its symmetry-driven vanishing, and its axis-dependence. Declare the symbols I_xy (signed, length^4), I_x and I_y (always positive for contrast), and element coordinates x and y. Name the exclusions: do not compute a numeric I_xy, do not assemble a composite by summing A_i x_i y_i, do not apply the parallel-axis transfer, do not construct Mohr's circle or compute a principal angle (owned by mohrs_circle_area_moment), do not re-derive the inclined-axis transformation (owned by inclined_axis_area_moment), and do not introduce mass or dynamics. Cite area_moment_of_inertia only for the contrast that I_x and I_y are always positive.

Interpret the SIGN of I_xy from quadrant placement. For each described region, determine whether x and y share a sign (first/third quadrants → integrand x y positive) or differ (second/fourth → integrand x y negative). Conclude I_xy > 0 or I_xy < 0 from that sign reasoning alone. Do not evaluate a numeric magnitude.

Apply the SYMMETRY ZERO CONDITION. Identify whether either the x-axis or the y-axis is an axis of symmetry of the area. If so, argue that each element pairs with a mirror element whose x y contribution is equal and opposite, so the contributions cancel and I_xy = 0. Name which axis is the symmetry axis used in the argument. State that either axis alone suffices. Do not compute the integral to reach zero.

Reason about AXIS DEPENDENCE. State that I_xy depends on the orientation of the axis pair. For a general area with nonzero I_xy about a reference pair, argue that as the axes rotate I_xy varies continuously and, because it can be positive at some orientations and negative at others, there must exist an orientation at which I_xy = 0 — the principal orientation. Name that orientation in words. Do not compute the angle and do not construct Mohr's circle.

State the interpretive consequence: because I_xy may be positive, negative, or zero while I_x and I_y are always positive, I_xy is the quantity that couples the two axes, and its vanishing is what defines the principal directions. Record the false converse: I_xy = 0 does not imply a symmetry axis, because a principal orientation of an asymmetric area also gives zero.

Verify before reporting by a consistency check of the three interpretive conclusions against each other, with no computation. Confirm that Cases 1–3 are mutually consistent under one principle — that I_xy is a signed, axis-dependent measure that symmetry can force to zero: Case 1 shows a nonzero signed value under asymmetric placement, Case 2 shows zero under symmetry, and Case 3 shows a rotation that reaches zero. Confirm none contradicts another: an area with a symmetry axis (Case 2) is already at a principal orientation (Case 3 with the vanishing orientation being the symmetry axis itself). Record the honest limitation: interpretation fixes sign and vanishing conditions, not magnitude; zero does not prove symmetry.

Report the three interpretive conclusions — sign from quadrant reasoning, zero from the named symmetry axis, and existence of a principal orientation where I_xy vanishes — without any computed I_xy value, composite assembly, parallel-axis transfer, Mohr construction, or principal angle. Stop.

signature.notes: Product of inertia — CONCEPTUAL interpretation, opening Batch 4N and the conceptual twin of the signed computational product_of_inertia_area in the same subtopic. This is the sharpest interpret-versus-compute reciprocal in the curriculum: the two nodes share a subtopic, the symbols I_xy, x and y, and the subject, differing only in that one computes and one interprets. Verified that every conclusion is reached by reasoning and none by computation — no integral evaluated, no composite A_i x_i y_i summed, no parallel-axis transfer applied, no numeric I_xy produced anywhere. Case 1 concludes I_xy > 0 for a first-quadrant area because the integrand x y is positive throughout, and I_xy < 0 for the second-quadrant reflection, from quadrant sign alone. Case 2 concludes I_xy = 0 for a centered rectangle by an element-level mirror argument — each element at (x, y) pairs with a mirror at (x, -y) whose contributions x y and -x y cancel — with the either-axis condition correctly stated that only one symmetry axis is required. Case 3 concludes a principal orientation where I_xy vanishes must EXIST, by a continuity argument that I_xy varies continuously under rotation and takes both signs, with the angle and construction explicitly ceded to mohrs_circle_area_moment — establishing why such an orientation exists without computing it. THE FALSE CONVERSE is the sharpest content and is precise: I_xy = 0 does not imply a symmetry axis, because a principal orientation of an asymmetric area also gives zero, and the artifact ties this back by noting that Case 2's symmetry axis is itself a principal orientation, so Cases 2 and 3 cohere rather than compete. The consistency-check verification confirms the three conclusions are three faces of one principle — signed when asymmetric, zero when symmetric, vanishing under rotation — with no computation, and the honest limitation records that interpretation fixes sign and vanishing conditions but not magnitude, which only the sibling's computation supplies, and that zero does not prove symmetry. No mass, no dynamics. Symbol reuse deliberate: I_xy, x, y reused with identical meaning from product_of_inertia_area; I_x, I_y cited for contrast; no binding of u, d, k, theta as a principal angle, m, M_O, A_gen or V, and no principal-angle symbol introduced. Three earned signals at distinct steps with the sign-versus-axis boundary argued: sign_or_placement_error at step 2 where the sign is read from the quadrant, axis_confusion at step 3 where the symmetry axis is identified and the either-axis condition applied, and unclassified at step 1 as the boundary fallback covering computing a value, constructing Mohr's circle, the false converse, claiming a magnitude, or introducing mass. simple_average_used and solution_sequencing_error cannot be earned. SCHEMA-FIT: the interpretive-relation form fits the formula field with populated variables the honest choice, since notation carries the sign rule, the symmetry zero condition, and the axis-dependence relation as conditions using I_xy, I_x, I_y, x and y — consistent with the two-pattern rule established across GENERAL_PRINCIPLES. Identify the angle reference axis and the quadrant in which the vector lies.

Compute the component magnitudes using sine and cosine with the given magnitude and angle.
Assign signs to F_x and F_y based on the vector direction and the axis convention.

ordered_steps: Establish a right-handed xyz frame and state the positive sense of each axis.

Project onto the relevant coordinate plane using the out-of-plane angle: assign the plane-projection magnitude and the axis-direction component with sine and cosine correctly for the stated reference (for φ from +z: F_xy = F sin φ and Fz = F cos φ). Do not skip this step and treat one angle as sufficient.
Resolve the in-plane projection into its two rectangular components using the second angle (for θ from +x in the xy-plane: |Fx| = F_xy cos θ and |Fy| = F_xy sin θ).
Assign algebraic signs to Fx, Fy, and Fz from the stated direction of the force relative to +x, +y, and +z.
Write the force in Cartesian form with units: F = Fx i + Fy j + Fz k.

Verify with the magnitude relation F^2 = Fx^2 + Fy^2 + Fz^2, then stop. Do not introduce coordinate direction angles, add other vectors, form position or unit vectors along a line, take a dot or cross product, draw an FBD, or write equilibrium equations.

ordered_steps: Identify the given 3D Cartesian vector A = Ax i + Ay j + Az k with known components. Cite cartesian_vector_components_3d as the inverse skill (angles into components) — do not re-derive a two-angle resolution here. Cite resultant_direction_2d as the 2D analogue.

Assign each component to its own axis angle: cos α = Ax/A with α measured from +x, cos β = Ay/A with β from +y, cos γ = Az/A with γ from +z. Do not swap which component feeds which angle.

Retain each component's algebraic sign in its cosine ratio. A negative component gives a negative cosine and an obtuse angle from that positive axis; a positive component gives an acute angle. Evaluate α = arccos(Ax/A), β = arccos(Ay/A), γ = arccos(Az/A).

Verify the identity cos²α + cos²β + cos²γ = 1. Note: because the identity sums squared cosines, it still closes if the components were assigned to the wrong axes or if a negative sign were dropped — it confirms component–magnitude consistency and does not catch an axis swap or a sign error.
Report all three angles with units (degrees to one decimal place unless the problem specifies otherwise).
Stop at α, β, and γ. Do not add vectors, form a position vector from two points, introduce a unit-vector symbol, or take a dot or cross product.

ordered_steps: Identify the two points A(xA, yA, zA) and B(xB, yB, zB). Cite cartesian_vector_components_3d for Cartesian form. Do not form a unit vector, a moment, a cross product, a dot product, a projection, a resultant by addition, or direction angles.
For each axis, difference only matching coordinates: x with x, y with y, z with z. Do not subtract across axes or assign a difference to the wrong unit vector.

Apply head-minus-tail in the directed sense FROM A TO B: r_AB = (xB − xA) i + (yB − yA) j + (zB − zA) k. Handle double negatives (subtracting a negative coordinate). State the order relation r_BA = −r_AB.
Compute |r_AB| as the straight-line distance. Do not treat the magnitude as distinguishing order or catching a sign slip — |r_AB| = |r_BA|, and a single flipped component leaves |r| unchanged.

Verify before reporting by reconstructing the head from the tail, component-wise: xA + (xB − xA) = xB, and likewise for y and z. This checks the differencing and its order; it is not a general vector-addition solve.
Report r_AB as a Cartesian vector and |r_AB| as the distance. Do not report a unit vector.
Stop. Do not normalize to a unit vector, compute a moment or cross product, form a dot product or projection, add vectors as a resultant, or extract direction angles.

ordered_steps: Identify the tail point A(xA, yA, zA) and the head point B(xB, yB, zB). State the required direction FROM A TO B. Cite position_vector_3d for the head-minus-tail construction — form r, then normalize; do not re-derive the position vector from first principles. Do not classify the quantity. Do not resolve by a stated angle. Do not scale u to obtain a force vector (force_directed_along_line). Do not form a dot product, a cross product, or a projection.
Assemble the components of r_AB on matching axes only: r_x from the x-coordinates, r_y from the y-coordinates, r_z from the z-coordinates. Do not transpose components between axes.
Form r_AB by head-minus-tail FROM A TO B: r_AB = (xB − xA, yB − yA, zB − zA). Handle subtraction of a negative coordinate. Do not take tail-minus-head.
Compute the magnitude |r_AB| = √(r_x² + r_y² + r_z²).

Normalize: u_AB = r_AB / |r_AB|. State that u_AB is dimensionless and that |u_AB| must equal one. Form the reversed-order result r_BA = −r_AB, |r_BA| = |r_AB|, and u_BA = −u_AB, and record that the order of the points is part of the answer.

Verify before reporting by a route that does not reuse the division: confirm (r_x/|r_AB|)² + (r_y/|r_AB|)² + (r_z/|r_AB|)² = 1, and confirm that metres divided by metres leaves u dimensionless. Record that this check cannot detect a reversed point order or a misread coordinate.
Report u_AB with the stated tail and head (FROM A TO B). Stop. Do not attach units to u, do not scale u to obtain a force vector, and do not form a dot product, a cross product, or a projection.

bindings.micro_skill: Computing centroid of composite areas using weighted averages

ordered_steps: Divide the composite area into simple sub-shapes (rectangles, circles, triangles).
Identify the reference coordinate axes (origin and positive x, y directions) stated in the problem.
For each sub-shape i: determine area Aᵢ and locate centroid coordinates (x̄ᵢ, ȳᵢ) measured from the reference axes.
Compute each part's contribution to Qx: Aᵢ·ȳᵢ (first moment about the x-axis).
Compute each part's contribution to Qy: Aᵢ·x̄ᵢ (first moment about the y-axis).
Sum all Aᵢ·ȳᵢ contributions to obtain Qx.
Sum all Aᵢ·x̄ᵢ contributions to obtain Qy.
Report Qx and Qy with area·length units (e.g., m³ or in³). Do not divide by total area — composite centroid location is a separate skill.

signature.notes: First moments of area Qx=ΣAᵢȳᵢ, Qy=ΣAᵢx̄ᵢ; setup-only, stops before ΣA division (composite_centroid owns that). 3-signal {sign_or_placement_error:3, simple_average_used:4, unclassified:8}. Worked example independently re-derived (Qx=10 m³, Qy=25 m³). Batch 4A routine under closed-field enforcement.

ordered_steps: Identify the reference coordinate system stated in the problem (origin and positive x, y directions).
Inspect the area boundary for candidate symmetry axes — lines about which one half of the area appears to mirror the other.
Test each candidate axis: confirm that reflecting the area across the axis reproduces the same shape (equal areas on both sides, matching boundary on both sides). Reject axes that fail this test.

For each confirmed symmetry axis, state the centroid consequence: identify which centroidal coordinate is fixed because the centroid must lie on that axis (vertical axis fixes x̄; horizontal axis fixes ȳ).
If two non-parallel confirmed symmetry axes exist, conclude the centroid lies at their intersection and report both coordinates if the intersection is known from geometry.

If only one symmetry axis is confirmed, report the fixed centroidal coordinate and explicitly state which coordinate is not determined by symmetry and would require first-moment or composite computation in a downstream skill.

Present the symmetry conclusion as the result for this skill. Do not perform first-moment summation, area decomposition tables, or division by total area unless the problem explicitly requires finding the remaining coordinate in this step.

ordered_steps: Divide the composite shape into simple sub-shapes (rectangles, circles, triangles).
Identify the reference axis (usually the bottom-left corner or a specified origin).
Calculate the area Aᵢ of each sub-shape.
Locate the centroid (xᵢ, yᵢ) of each sub-shape from the reference axis.
Compute the moment for each sub-shape: Aᵢxᵢ and Aᵢyᵢ.
Sum all moments: ΣAᵢxᵢ and ΣAᵢyᵢ.
Sum all areas: ΣAᵢ.
Divide: x̄ = ΣAᵢxᵢ / ΣAᵢ and ȳ = ΣAᵢyᵢ / ΣAᵢ.

actions: Identify planes or axes of symmetry for the primitive.
Conclude that the centroid lies on each symmetry feature.
Assign zero or centered coordinates only relative to the chosen origin.
ordered_steps.reasoning: Symmetry reduces the number of coordinates that must be computed.
ordered_steps.title: Mark all symmetry planes, axes, or centers

actions: Use the primitive lookup rule when the solid matches a standard shape.
Use x_bar = (1/V) ∫ x dV (and y, z analogs) only when integration is required.
Do not use composite centroid summation for a single primitive.
ordered_steps.reasoning: Standard primitive locations are faster and less error-prone than integration when they apply.
ordered_steps.title: Select the correct primitive centroid rule or volume centroid formula

actions: Measure axial distances from the stated base, flat face, or center—not an assumed default.
For a cone, use h/4 from the base or 3h/4 from the apex consistently with the problem statement.
For a hemisphere, use 3R/8 from the flat face along the axis of symmetry.
ordered_steps.reasoning: Centroid coordinates are meaningless unless referenced to the problem coordinate system.
ordered_steps.title: Measure centroid coordinates from the stated origin/reference face

actions: Set coordinates to zero on symmetry planes through the origin when applicable.
Compute only the remaining coordinate(s) from the primitive rule.
Keep units consistent throughout.
ordered_steps.reasoning: Symmetry often fixes one or more centroid coordinates without calculation.
ordered_steps.title: Assign zero or centered coordinates using symmetry where appropriate

actions: Report (x_bar, y_bar, z_bar) with units from the problem origin.
Verify the centroid lies on expected symmetry axes.
Confirm the result is a volume centroid, not an area or composite centroid.
ordered_steps.reasoning: The answer must lie inside the solid and match the stated reference frame.
ordered_steps.title: State the final centroid coordinates and check physical consistency

ordered_steps: Identify the composite body, the stated reference planes, and the required axes. Decompose into volumetric primitives. Take each primitive's volume V_i and its own centroid coordinates as GIVEN from centroid_volume_primitives — do not re-derive them. Cite composite_centroid as the area counterpart of the same weighting logic (do not re-derive it) and centroid_first_moments for the first-moment idea (do not re-derive it). Do not integrate. Do not use revolution methods. Do not introduce mass or density.
Record V_1, V_2 and the given centroids (x_1, y_1, z_1), (x_2, y_2, z_2). Form the total volume V = V_1 + V_2.

For each required axis, pair only the matching centroid coordinate into that axis's first-moment sum: x_i with the x-sum, z_i with the z-sum. Do not place an x-coordinate into the z-sum or a z-coordinate into the x-sum.
Form the first moments of volume V_i x_i and V_i z_i, sum them, and divide by V to obtain x̄ and z̄. Do not average the primitive centroid coordinates without volume weights.

State ȳ by symmetry when every primitive shares the same y-centroid on that axis. Screen the result by comparing the unweighted averages of the x- and z-coordinates to the volume-weighted x̄ and z̄ so the gap is visible.

Verify before reporting by reaching x̄ from a different reference plane and transferring back to the original reference. Record that agreement confirms consistent weighting and division, not the given primitive inputs.
Report x̄, ȳ, and z̄ with the stated references and units. Stop. Do not integrate, do not introduce mass or density, and do not reach into revolution methods.

signature.notes: Centroid of a composite volume as the volume-weighted assembly of volumetric primitives. Independently re-derived: V_1 = 192000 mm^3 at (60, 40, 10) and V_2 = 96000 mm^3 at (20, 40, 35), volumes differing by a factor of two; V = 288000 mm^3. First moments about x = 0: 11520000 + 1920000 = 13440000 mm^4, x-bar = 46.6667 mm reported as 46.67 mm with the rounding stated. About z = 0: 1920000 + 3360000 = 5280000 mm^4, z-bar = 18.3333 mm reported as 18.33 mm with the rounding stated. y-bar = 40 mm stated by symmetry rather than the axis being silently omitted. Discrimination confirmed live rather than asserted: the unweighted average of the x-coordinates is 40 mm against the weighted 46.67 mm, and on z is 22.5 mm against 18.33 mm, gaps that exist precisely because the volumes differ. ordered_steps: Identify the generating CURVE, a non-intersecting axis of revolution in its plane, and the angle θ in radians. State the first theorem: surface area from revolving a curve about that axis. Complement (named only): pappus_guldinus_volume owns revolving a plane area about an axis to generate volume using the area centroid — do not compute that volume and do not introduce a generating-area or volume quantity. Cite centroid_first_moments for the curve centroid as given. Do not integrate. Do not introduce mass or density.

Record the curve length L and identify the centroid OF THE CURVE. Measure r̄_c as the perpendicular distance from the axis to that line centroid. Do not substitute the centroid of an area bounded by the curve.
Compute A = θ · r̄_c · L with θ in radians. Confirm dimensions: length × length × dimensionless → length².

When a related area centroid of the same shape is available for screening, report the incorrect surface area that would result from using that area-centroid distance with the same L and θ, so the gap from the curve-centroid result is visible.

Verify before reporting, when the curve is parallel to the axis at constant distance, by an elementary cylindrical-surface route that does not reuse the theorem. Record that this check is special to constant-distance generators and does not validate centroid inputs in general.
Report A with the axis, θ in radians, and units. Stop. Do not compute a volume, do not use degrees for θ, and do not integrate.

signature.notes: First theorem of Pappus-Guldinus, surface area generated by revolving a plane CURVE about a non-intersecting axis, A = theta * r_bar_c * L with theta in radians. Independently re-derived. Case 1: a segment of length 60 mm parallel to the axis at constant 40 mm, revolved through pi/2, gives A = (pi/2)(40)(60) = 1200 pi = 3769.91 mm^2. Verified by an independent elementary route that does not reuse the theorem: the swept surface is a quarter of a cylindrical lateral surface of radius 40 and height 60, whose full area is 2 pi (40)(60) = 4800 pi, one quarter of which is 1200 pi — an exact match. Case 2 carries the discrimination: the hypotenuse of a 30-40-50 right triangle placed with vertices at (30, 0), (60, 0) and (30, 40), revolved about x = 0. Both centroid distances were re-derived from those vertices: hypotenuse length sqrt(900 + 1600) = 50 mm, curve centroid at the midpoint (45, 20) giving r_bar_c = 45 mm, and the centroid of the triangular AREA at the vertex average (40, 13.33) giving 40 mm. A = (pi/2)(45)(50) = 1125 pi = 3534.29 mm^2 from the curve centroid, against 1000 pi = 3141.59 mm^2 from the area centroid — a gap of 125 pi, about 11 percent, making the line-centroid versus area-centroid distinction visible numerically rather than asserted in prose. The axis does not intersect the triangle, all of whose points lie at x >= 30. Theta is stated in radians and a quarter revolution is used so that theta is a visible variable rather than an invisible 2 pi; the dimensional argument that degrees cannot produce a correct area is recorded. Verified excluded — no volume is computed anywhere, no generating-area or volume symbol is introduced, and the complement is named in exactly one sentence so a student can distinguish the theorems without this artifact performing the other. centroid_first_moments supplies the curve centroid, taken as given and not re-derived; composite weighting for segmented curves is owned elsewhere; the theorem replaces integration; no mass or density. ordered_steps: Identify the generating AREA, a non-intersecting axis of revolution in its plane, and the angle θ in radians. State the second theorem: volume from revolving a plane area about that axis using the area centroid. Complement (named only): pappus_guldinus_surface_area owns revolving a plane CURVE about an axis to generate surface area using the curve's line centroid — do not compute that surface area and do not introduce a generated-surface-area or curve-length quantity. Distinct from centroid_composite_volumes (assembly of known primitive volumes — do not assemble a composite here). Cite centroid_first_moments / composite_centroid / standard results for the area centroid as given. Do not integrate. Do not introduce mass or density.

Record the generating area A_gen and identify the centroid OF THAT AREA. Measure r̄_a as the perpendicular distance from the axis to that area centroid. Do not substitute the centroid of the bounding curve.
Compute V = θ · r̄_a · A_gen with θ in radians. Confirm dimensions: dimensionless × length × length² → length³.

When a related line centroid of the same shape's boundary is available for screening, report the incorrect volume that would result from using that curve-centroid distance with the same A_gen and θ, so the gap from the area-centroid result is visible.

Verify before reporting by a consistency check that does not claim an independent geometric route: compute the full-revolution volume from the same theorem, V_full = 2π · r̄_a · A_gen, and confirm the partial result equals (θ / 2π) of that full volume. Record plainly that this ratio check reuses the theorem and the same centroid, so it confirms linear dependence on θ and arithmetic consistency but does NOT independently validate V or r̄_a.
Report V with the axis, θ in radians, and units. Stop. Do not compute a surface area, do not use degrees for θ, do not integrate, and do not assemble a composite volume.

ordered_steps: Confirm the load diagram decomposes into standard shapes (rectangle, triangle, or trapezoid as rectangle plus triangle) — not a uniform-only load (defer to simple_distributed_load_resultant) and not a continuous w(x) requiring integration (defer to general_distributed_load_resultant).
Establish a position coordinate x along the span, state the origin from which locations will be measured, and identify the loaded interval.
Decompose the load diagram into non-overlapping standard parts (typically a rectangle plus a triangle for a trapezoidal load).
For each part i, compute its load area R_i (rectangle: w × L; triangle: ½ × base × height intensity).

For each part i, locate the part centroid x_i using the standard-shape rule (rectangle: midpoint; triangle: the centroid lies at b/3 measured from the maximum-intensity end, equivalently 2b/3 from the zero-intensity end).
Sum part magnitudes R = Σ R_i and compute the area-weighted line of action x_bar = Σ(R_i · x_i) / R.
State the direction of R (the same direction as the distributed load unless the problem states otherwise).

Report the equivalent resultant with magnitude, direction, line-of-action location x_bar relative to the stated origin, and units; sanity-check that R has force units, x_bar lies within the loaded span, and no part was double-counted or omitted.

bindings.micro_skill: Identifying force types and directions

ordered_steps: State the complement: unit_vector_along_line builds the direction; this skill scales it by a magnitude into a force. Identify the scalar magnitude F and the required direction FROM the stated tail A(xA,yA,zA) TO the stated head B(xB,yB,zB). Take u_AB as given or cite its construction from r_AB and |r_AB|; do not re-derive normalization as the objective. Do not project a vector onto a direction (dot_product_projection). Do not form a moment. Do not write equilibrium equations or a reaction inventory.

Obtain u_AB for the stated FROM-A-TO-B direction. Form the force components by multiplying F by each unit-vector component on matching axes only: F_x with the x-component of u_AB, F_y with the y-component, F_z with the z-component. Do not transpose components between axes or pair F with a mismatched unit-vector component.

Assemble F_vec = F u_AB. Confirm the direction matches the stated tail and head. Form the reversed-order contrast: u_BA = −u_AB gives F u_BA = −F_vec — every component negated. Record that the point order is part of the answer.

Verify before reporting by a route that does not reuse the multiplication: compute |F_vec| from its components and confirm it equals F; also confirm F_vec / F recovers u_AB. Record that the magnitude check cannot detect a reversed point order and does not validate the given F or the endpoint coordinates.
Report F_vec with units and the stated tail and head (FROM A TO B). Stop.

signature.notes: Force of known magnitude directed along a line expressed as a Cartesian vector, F_vec = F u_AB. Independently re-derived: |r_AB| = sqrt(16 + 144 + 9) = sqrt(169) = 13 m; u_AB = (4/13, -12/13, 3/13), mixed sign on all three axes; 390 / 13 = 30 exactly, so F_vec = (120, -360, 90) N, whose components are clean integers visibly distinct from the unit-vector fractions so that the unit vector cannot be mistaken for the force. Verified by a route independent of the multiplication: |F_vec| = sqrt(14400 + 129600 + 8100) = sqrt(152100) = 390 N, recovering the given scalar, and F_vec / 390 = (4/13, -12/13, 3/13) recovering u_AB. Reversed-order contrast confirmed: u_BA = -u_AB gives (-120, 360, -90) N, every component negated, establishing that the point order is part of the answer. RECIPROCAL BOUNDARY, the central requirement and cleanly met: unit_vector_along_line, the signed prerequisite, builds the direction and explicitly excluded the force multiplication, reserving it here; this skill completes the handoff by scaling the cited unit vector into a force without re-deriving the normalization as the objective, with the complement named in one sentence. dot_product_projection shares the topic and is excluded — no projection and no dot product appears, this skill building a force vector rather than projecting one; no moment is formed; no equilibrium equations or reaction inventory. Symbol continuity: u_AB, u_BA, r_AB, |r_AB| and the point coordinate names reused with identical meaning from unit_vector_along_line and position_vector_3d, with scalar F and F_vec introduced and F declared explicitly as a scalar magnitude distinct from the vector F bound by the moment skills; bare u not rebound. Three earned signals at distinct steps: axis_confusion at step 2 where axis-matched products are formed and transposition is the failure, sign_or_placement_error at step 3 where the vector is assembled and the point order fixed and reversal is the failure, and unclassified at step 1 as the boundary fallback. simple_average_used cannot be earned, not a Centroids-family skill. solution_sequencing_error omitted: F_vec cannot form before u_AB exists, so an ordering dependence is real, but the chain is strictly linear with no branching stranded unknown — the same disposition reached for unit_vector_along_line, and the correct ground, though the draft report worded it loosely as the dependence being absorbed into obtaining the direction; the omission is correct and is recorded here with the cleaner justification. Honest limitation recorded in the artifact: the magnitude check confirms the scalar was multiplied through consistently and that the unit vector had magnitude one, but cannot detect a reversed point order, since the opposite force also has magnitude 390 N, and does not validate the given magnitude or the endpoint coordinates; direction must be checked against the stated tail and head.

ordered_steps: Identify the given Cartesian vectors A (to be projected) and B (direction). Cite cartesian_vector_components_3d for components. Do not form a unit direction, a position vector, direction angles, a resultant by addition, a moment, or a cross product.
Pair like components and form the product sum A · B = Ax Bx + Ay By + Az Bz. Do not multiply across axes (Ax with By, for example).
Compute |A| and |B|. Form the signed scalar projection A_par = (A · B) / |B|, retaining the algebraic sign of A · B and using |B| — not |A| — as the divisor.
Recover cos θ = (A · B) / (|A| |B|) and θ. A negative A_par means θ is obtuse and A has a component opposite to B.

Verify before reporting: if A and B are not parallel, confirm |A_par| < |A|. This bound catches an undivided product sum and a sign-dropped product sum that is not strictly less than |A|; it does not catch dividing by |A| instead of |B|.
Report A_par (signed scalar projection) and θ. Do not report a vector projection.
Stop. Do not form a unit vector, a vector projection, a moment, a cross product, a position vector, direction angles, or a resultant by addition.

signature.notes: Batch 4I skill 4/5. Owns the dot product AS A PROJECTION TOOL: the component form A . B = Ax Bx + Ay By + Az Bz, the geometric form A . B = |A||B| cos theta, and the signed SCALAR projection of A onto the direction of B, A_par = (A . B)/|B|, including what a negative projection means (obtuse theta; A has a component opposite to B). Boundary: cartesian_vector_components_3d (signed parent) supplies components, cited not re-derived. RECIPROCAL BOUNDARY with cross_product_moment_3d (signed earlier this batch) is stated in the artifact: that skill uses a dot product ONLY as a perpendicularity check and computes no projection, while this skill owns the dot product as a projection tool and computes no moment or cross product - naming the complement was required because the sibling already states its half. unit_vector_along_line (downstream, planned) owns FORMING a unit direction; this skill uses the general form (A . B)/|B|, which needs no unit vector, and never binds or constructs one. The VECTOR projection (scalar times a unit direction) therefore requires that ceded construction and is explicitly OUT OF SCOPE - the deliverable is the signed SCALAR projection. position_vector_3d, coordinate_direction_angles and cartesian_vector_addition_3d excluded. Worked example Operator-re-derived from the on-disk prompt: A = -6i -6j -3k (|A| = 9), B = 2i +2j -1k (|B| = 3); A . B = (-6)(2) + (-6)(2) + (-3)(-1) = -12 - 12 + 3 = -21; A_par = -21/3 = -7; cos theta = -21/27 = -7/9 = -0.7778 -> theta = 141.1 deg. Distinguishing feature bites: the geometry is neither parallel nor perpendicular and theta sits clear of both 90 and 180 degrees; the projection is NEGATIVE so its sign carries meaning and the obtuse angle explains it; |A| != |B| so dividing by the wrong magnitude is detectable; and the four outcomes are mutually distinct - correct -7, wrong denominator -2.33, undivided -21, signs dropped +9 - so each mapped signal routes to its own answer. VERIFICATION PRECEDES REPORT in both arrays (verify at index 5, report at index 6), matching the three skills signed earlier in this batch: the bound |A_par| < |A|, valid because A and B are not parallel, gives 7 < 9. HONEST LIMITATION recorded: the bound catches an undivided product sum (21 > 9) and a sign-dropped product sum (27/3 = 9, not strictly less than 9) but does NOT catch dividing by |A| instead of |B| (2.33 < 9 passes while being wrong) - stated as a property of the check rather than overstated. THREE-signal mapping: axis_confusion at step 2 (like-component pairing in the product sum - multiplying Ax by By or Az by Bx), sign_or_placement_error at step 3 (sign retention through the division AND selection of |B| rather than |A| as the divisor, since dividing by |A| projects the wrong way round and is a placement error about which vector is the direction; both acts are explicitly authored in that step, distinct from the pairing act at step 2), unclassified at step 7 (report and boundary - incomplete result, omitted sign, skipped bound check, treating the bound as catching a wrong-denominator error, forming a unit vector or vector projection, or reaching into the ceded siblings). solution_sequencing_error OMITTED with explicit argument: A . B and |B| are independent computations combined by one division, so no authored step strands a prerequisite unknown; it was not mapped merely because the division follows the dot product. simple_average_used omitted (Centroids-family). Trig-resolution cross-check N/A recorded affirmatively: components are given already resolved and no inclined vector is decomposed. Operator observation recorded, not corrected: the bound-check step cites a sign-dropped sum of 27 without restating that 27 is the sum of the product magnitudes from two steps earlier - terse but inferable, and the instructional point of the sentence lands. ordered_steps: Identify the moment center O and choose the sign convention (counterclockwise positive, clockwise negative).
Identify the force, either by magnitude and direction or by components F_x and F_y.
Form the position vector r = <x, y> from O to a point on the force's line of action.
Compute the scalar moment M_O = x*F_y - y*F_x, or use +/- F*d if the perpendicular moment arm d is known.
Apply the sign convention: positive is counterclockwise, negative is clockwise.
Report the moment magnitude, rotational sense, and units (for example, N*m).
Sanity-check that the sign and sense match the physical rotation the force produces about O.

For each output axis, pair the correct r- and F-components in the cofactor cross terms: i uses (ry, Fz) and (rz, Fy); j uses (rx, Fz) and (rz, Fx); k uses (rx, Fy) and (ry, Fx). Do not swap which components feed which axis.

Apply the alternating minus on the j-cofactor and assemble M_O = (ry Fz − rz Fy) i − (rx Fz − rz Fx) j + (rx Fy − ry Fx) k. State the operand-order property: F × r = −M_O (reversing the operands reverses the moment's sense).
Verify perpendicularity before reporting: compute M_O · r = 0 and M_O · F = 0. Use the dot product only for this check — do not compute a projection.
Report M_O as a Cartesian vector with units. Do not headline the magnitude of M_O unless the problem asks for it.
Stop. Do not reduce about a specified axis, introduce a couple, form a force–couple system, or treat the check dots as projection work.

ordered_steps: Select the point O about which the moment is taken. State that M_O = r × F uses the cross product owned by cross_product_moment_3d and does not re-derive determinant expansion as the objective. Contrast moment_of_force_scalar_2d (planar signed scalar). Exclude projection onto a specified axis, scalar triple products, couples, equilibrium equations, and reaction inventories.

Identify the force F and its line of action. Confirm that each candidate point used for a position vector lies on that line — for example by checking that the segment between two candidates is parallel to F. A position vector to a point not on the line of action is invalid.
Construct a position vector from O to a point on the line of action: r points from the moment point toward the line, not from the force toward O. Record its Cartesian components (rx, ry, rz).
Form M_O = r × F using the Cartesian cross product from cross_product_moment_3d; record the resulting components. Do not treat determinant expansion as a new procedure to learn here.

Construct a second, visibly different position vector from O to another point on the SAME line of action. Form M_O again and confirm the two moment vectors are identical — the line-of-action invariance.

Interpret M_O: report its magnitude; identify the AXIS through O along the direction of M_O (unit direction if useful); state the SENSE by the right-hand rule; explain any zero component as the absence of rotational tendency about that coordinate axis through O, not as an error.

ordered_steps: Select a candidate member and list every point at which an external force acts on it: pin connections, applied loads, applied couples, and weight if weight is not neglected.

Apply the qualification test: exactly two loaded points; no force applied between those points; no couple applied to the member; weight neglected or negligible. If the test fails, state the disqualifier and do not treat the member as a two-force member.

For a member that passes: identify the two application points and draw the straight line joining them (the chord). If the member is bent or curved, do not follow the member's shape — the line of action is the chord, not the centerline of the bar.

State the equilibrium argument without computing values: moments about one application point vanish for the force at the other point only if that force's line of action passes through the first point, so the two forces are collinear along the chord; force equilibrium then requires them equal and opposite.
Label each force along the chord with an assumed sense (tension or compression). Do not compute a magnitude.

Report which candidates qualify, which do not (naming each disqualifier), and the force direction on each qualifying member. Stop: do not solve for magnitudes, do not invoke three-force concurrency, do not disassemble a frame or machine for analysis, and do not go 3D.

ordered_steps: Select each candidate body and list every external action on it: pin and roller reactions, applied loads, applied couples, and weight if weight is not neglected.

Apply the qualification test: exactly three forces; coplanar; no applied couple; weight neglected or counted as one of the three. If the test fails, name the disqualifier and do not treat the body as a three-force member.

For a body that passes: identify the known force lines of action. Extend two non-parallel known lines until they meet; call that intersection the concurrency point O. If the two known lines are parallel, recognize the degenerate case (concurrency at infinity) and stop without inventing a finite intersection.

State the concurrency argument without computing values: moments about O vanish for the two forces whose lines already pass through O, so equilibrium requires the third force's moment about O to vanish, which means its line of action must also pass through O.

Draw the third force through its application point and through O. Report its DIRECTION from that geometry (for example as a unit direction or as an angle from a stated axis). Do not compute a magnitude.

Report which candidates qualify, which do not (naming each disqualifier), and the direction of the previously unknown force on each qualifying body. Stop: do not solve ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0, or ΣM = 0 for magnitudes; do not build a force triangle or invoke Lami's theorem; do not disassemble a frame or machine; do not run a truss method; do not re-author the support catalog; do not go 3D.

ordered_steps: State the complement: constraints_static_determinacy counts reactions against equations; this skill examines the geometric arrangement of a body that already PASSES the count test. Take count-adequacy (n_r = n_e) as GIVEN — do not re-author the count test. Take the reaction inventory from the FBD skills; do not re-author the inventory. For each count-adequate body, examine reaction ARRANGEMENT. Test for the parallel failure mode: if all reactions are parallel, the body cannot resist a force perpendicular to that family — verdict improperly constrained.

Test for the concurrent failure mode: if all reaction lines of action pass through a single common point O (or, in 3D, intersect a common axis), the body cannot resist a moment about that point (or axis) — verdict improperly constrained.

If the reactions are neither all parallel nor all concurrent — components in two independent directions are present and the lines of action do not share one common point — verdict properly constrained. Record that the same n_r = n_e count can accompany either improper or proper arrangement.

Verify before reporting by an arrangement test that sets the count aside: ask (1) whether the reactions include components in two independent directions, and (2) whether the reaction lines of action fail to share a common point. Proper constraint requires BOTH answers yes. Confirm the same verdicts without counting. Record that the screen detects the classic improper modes, not every conceivable instability.
Report each body's arrangement verdict (improper-parallel, improper-concurrent, or proper) with the arrangement reason. Stop. Do not report reaction magnitudes.

signature.notes: Improper constraint detection — a body may pass the count-based determinacy test yet be unable to hold equilibrium because its reactions are arranged all parallel or all concurrent, so a correct reaction count is necessary but not sufficient for proper constraint. THE EQUAL-COUNT CONSTRUCTION IS THE SPINE AND IT HOLDS: all three worked bodies carry n_r = n_e = 3 and pass the count test identically, so arrangement alone separates the verdicts and the skill does not collapse into the determinacy test it extends. Body A, a beam on three vertical rollers, is improper by PARALLEL reactions — with no horizontal reaction component, sum Fx = 0 becomes 0 = the horizontal load and cannot be satisfied, so the beam slides. Body B, a plate held by three links whose lines of action all pass through a common point O, is improper by CONCURRENT reactions — producing no moment about O, sum M about O = 0 becomes 0 = the applied moment about O and cannot be satisfied, so the plate rotates. Each improper mode is made concrete as an equilibrium equation that cannot be satisfied rather than asserted. Body C, a pin plus roller at the SAME count of three, is proper: the pin supplies two independent directions and the roller keeps the lines non-concurrent, so a horizontal load and a moment both find resistance. The arrangement test verifies all three verdicts WITHOUT counting, by two questions — are components present in two independent directions, and do the reaction lines fail to share a common point — with proper constraint requiring both yes: Body A fails the first, Body B the second, Body C passes both. BOUNDARY: constraints_static_determinacy, the signed prerequisite and subtopic sibling, owns the count test, which is cited and taken as given and not re-authored, the complement stated in one sentence that it counts reactions against equations while this skill examines the arrangement of a body that already passes that count. The reaction inventory is taken from the FBD skills, and this artifact explicitly completes the deferral recorded in rigid_body_fbd_3d that six unknowns do not imply proper constraint. No reaction values are solved; improper constraint is detected from geometry as inconsistent or indeterminate equilibrium equations for a general load. The common point O is declared distinct from a computed moment point M_O. Honest limitation recorded: the arrangement screen catches the classic all-parallel and all-concurrent modes for a count-adequate planar body and is not a general proof of stability for every loading, with complex 3D mixed cases possibly needing fuller analysis — passing the screen means the classic improper modes are absent, not that every instability is excluded. One earned signal, unclassified at step 1, the boundary and method fallback for concluding proper constraint from count alone, re-authoring the count test, solving for reactions, or skipping the arrangement exam. axis_confusion was scrutinized specifically, since the parallel and concurrent modes concern directions and lines of action, and correctly omitted: the failure this skill guards against is not examining arrangement at all, a method error caught at step 1, rather than misreading which axis is involved, so mapping axis_confusion onto a geometric-reasoning skill would be padding. sign_or_placement_error, simple_average_used and solution_sequencing_error cannot be earned: no signed quantity or force placement authored, no averaging, and no stranded prerequisite chain. This draft required no correction, the fourth consecutive clean draft, and its artifact was re-delivered in full for the review beat after the lane-closure notice arrived without it.

bindings.micro_skill: Sketching shear and bending-moment diagrams for a determinate beam with one concentrated load using piecewise values along the span

ordered_steps: State the load-shear-moment relations to be used: dV/dx = −w, dM/dx = V, and the area forms ΔV = −∫ w dx, ΔM = ∫ V dx. State the sign convention (w positive downward; V and M matching the internal-loading siblings).

Identify the span or region of interest and obtain any needed point values of V or M at a section by citing shear_force_internal_loading / bending_moment_internal_loading (or given values). Do not re-solve single-cut equilibrium here.
Where a distributed load acts, apply dV/dx = −w to obtain the shear slope. Keep the minus: a downward load (w > 0) gives a negative shear slope (V decreases along +x).

Between two sections, apply ΔV = −∫ w dx (area under the load diagram; cite the area-under-w idea from general_distributed_load_resultant when useful) and/or ΔM = ∫ V dx (area under the shear diagram) as required. Do not draw the complete V and M diagrams across the whole beam.

Locate (or reason about) any interior point where V = 0 in the region of interest and state that M has a local extremum there because dM/dx = V = 0. Do not treat max |w| or max |V| as the moment-extremum locator, and do not compute the numeric global maximum moment as this skill's deliverable.

Report the applied relation results (slope, ΔV and/or ΔM, and/or the V = 0 extremum location). Stop before constructing full shear/moment diagrams and before specializing in the numeric global max moment.

signature.notes: Batch 4G skill 2/5. Scope Operator-derived. The load-shear-moment relationship node: owns the differential relations dV/dx = -w and dM/dx = V and their area forms (ΔV = -area under w; ΔM = area under V), plus the consequences (V=0 -> M local extremum; concentrated load -> V jump; couple -> M jump; unloaded span V constant M linear; uniform load V linear M parabolic). Worked example Operator-re-derived: 6 m simply-supported beam, uniform w=4 kN/m, Ay=By=12, V(0+)=12. dV/dx = -w = -4 kN/m (the minus is load-bearing: downward w gives decreasing shear; +4 would reverse the sense and misplace the extremum). ΔV = -area under w = -(4)(6) = -24 kN, checked V(6-)=12-24=-12. V(x)=12-4x, V=0 at x=3 m, where dM/dx=V=0 so M has a local extremum - and the example states the extremum is NOT at max|w| or max|V| (which are at the ends), the exact misconception the skill owns. All deliverables are local/span relation applications; no full diagram drawn, no numeric M_max computed. TWO-signal mapping: sign_or_placement_error at step 3 (the dV/dx=-w sign and the V=0 extremum placement - the skill's crux), unclassified at step 6 (the diagram/max-moment boundary). axis_confusion OMITTED: a calculus-relation skill, no component-resolution step. solution_sequencing_error OMITTED although the w->V->M integration has a natural order and this was the batch skill where it could plausibly be earned: considered honestly and declined - no authored step exposes an out-of-order solve that strands a prerequisite unknown with direct evidence; the example applies the relations in order without a sequencing trap. The fifth signal is mapped only where an authored step earns it, not defaulted because integration has an order. simple_average_used omitted (Centroids-family). ordered_steps: Obtain support reactions if they are not given (cite beam_reactions). Do not re-teach the support-type catalog.

Cite the load-shear-moment relations from shear_moment_load_relationships (dV/dx = −w, dM/dx = V, area forms, jump rules, degree rules). State the sign convention. Do not re-derive the relations from first principles.

Construct the complete shear diagram left to right across the whole beam: start just left of the leftmost force, apply a jump at each concentrated reaction or load, apply slope −w under distributed load, and hold V constant on unloaded segments. Record V at every key point (supports, load boundaries, concentrated forces, and where V = 0). Verify closure: V returns to zero after the last vertical reaction.

Only after the shear diagram is fully determined at every key point, construct the moment diagram from the area under V (ΔM = ∫ V dx) and the degree rules. Do not attempt the M diagram before the V diagram exists — without V, the areas that determine ΔM are unavailable. Building M first (or by re-solving ΣM at many cuts instead of using area-under-V) strands that prerequisite.

Construct the complete moment diagram: integrate / accumulate areas under V segment by segment, apply the correct degree (linear V → parabolic M under uniform load), and enforce closure (M = 0 at simple-support or free ends). Record M at every key point, including the station where V = 0.

On the finished diagrams, mark where V = 0 and the M value there as the diagram peak. Do not reframe the deliverable as extracting the numeric global maximum moment alone — that specialization belongs to maximum_moment_from_zero_shear.

Report the complete V and M diagrams by their key-point values and segment shapes/degrees. Stop — do not treat global-max-M extraction as this skill's deliverable, and do not replace traversal with per-point section equilibrium.

M from area under V - M(0)=0, area 0-3 = +(1/2)(3)(12)=18 -> M(3)=18, area 3-6 = -18 -> M(6)=0, closes at the simple support, parabolic under UDL. Peak M=18 kN·m at x=3 where V=0. ordered_steps: Obtain the finished shear diagram (and moment values at key points if already available) from shear_moment_diagram_construction. Cite that skill; do not make reconstructing the complete diagrams the deliverable of this skill.

Cite dM/dx = V from shear_moment_load_relationships: interior moment extrema occur where V = 0. State that the global maximum is the largest |M| among all candidates, not automatically the first V = 0 station found.
List every candidate station: all locations where V = 0, plus supports, free ends, and any concentrated-couple discontinuity that can carry a moment jump.

Evaluate M at each candidate (read from the given moment diagram, or compute as the cumulative area under V from a known M = 0 reference). Include both positive (sagging) and negative (hogging) values.
Compare the magnitudes |M| at all candidates. Select the largest |M| as the global maximum moment; record its signed value, location x, and sense (sagging or hogging).

signature.notes: Batch 4G skill 4/5. Scope Operator-derived. The tightest-boundary skill in the chain: extracts the numeric GLOBAL maximum bending moment from a GIVEN finished diagram, consuming shear_moment_diagram_construction (skill 3) as input rather than re-constructing it. Owns exactly the sliver skill 3 ceded. Candidates compared by magnitude: |M(3)|=18 vs |M(8)|=32 -> GLOBAL MAX = -32 kN·m hogging at x=8 (support B). The first V=0 station (x=3, +18) is deliberately NOT the answer - the overhang produces a larger hogging support moment, so the >=2-candidate comparison and the include-hogging rule genuinely bite (a single-hump SS beam would not exercise the skill). bindings.micro_skill: Adding vectors by components

ordered_steps: Identify each quantity Q to classify. Treat classification as a property of the quantity, not of notation or of whether a stated number carries a sign. Do not classify by the ingredients Q is built from. State the two independent criteria (specification test and combination test). Choose no axes; do not compute components; do not resolve, add, or decompose vectors; do not build a unit vector.
Apply the specification test to each Q: fully specified by magnitude and units alone → SCALAR; additionally requires a direction before it is determined → VECTOR.

Apply the combination test independently to each Q: combine by arithmetic addition of signed magnitudes on a single scale → SCALAR; require head-to-tail composition whose sum depends on the angle between the parts → VECTOR. Do not treat sign cancellation on a line as the vector test.

Confirm that the two criteria agree for each Q. If they disagree, revise the identification of Q or the application of a test. Record that agreement confirms consistent application only — it is not external validation of the classification.
Verify before reporting: re-apply the combination test independently to work and to moment of a force, and confirm each reaches the same classification the specification test already gave.

Report each Q as SCALAR or VECTOR with the stated reason from the criteria. Stop. Do not resolve, add, or decompose vectors; do not choose axes; do not build a unit vector; do not report a bare label without a reason.

signature.notes: Scalar-versus-vector classification on two independent criteria required to agree. First draft BLOCKED on Operator review for a criterion defect: the combination test was authored as "sum magnitude can be less than either part", which the artifact's own signed scalar satisfies, since -8 C and +8 C sum to zero by arithmetic cancellation. The criterion therefore failed to discriminate and the moment verification reached a correct answer by reasoning that would misclassify a scalar. Corrected under PHASE-D-SCALAR-VECTOR-CLASSIFICATION-CURSOR-CORRECTION-001: the discriminator is now dependence on the ANGLE between parts in head-to-tail composition, which has no scalar counterpart, and sign cancellation on a line is explicitly excluded as a vector test. Independently checked against the signed case: -8 and +8 cancel on a single scale with no angle and classify SCALAR correctly under the restated criterion. Moment case now concedes that same-axis moments combine by signed arithmetic and locates the vector property in non-parallel-axis directional composition, with that composition owned by cross_product_moment_3d and moment_of_force_vector_3d and NOT authored here; the artifact records that the worked example does not exercise non-parallel axes. Discriminating pairs verified present and biting: work SCALAR versus moment VECTOR defeats classification by ingredients; distance versus displacement defeats classification by magnitude and units; the signed temperature change defeats sign as a vector test. Signal set is one earned signal, unclassified, retargeted from step 6 to step 1 per Architect ruling MAPPING_DEFECT / NOT_NEW_SIGNAL, step 1 being the earliest general recovery step stating both criteria. axis_confusion and solution_sequencing_error recorded as CANNOT BE EARNED by any authored step: no axis is chosen and criteria order is free. sign_or_placement_error and simple_average_used unearned, not trimmed. Honest limitation recorded in the artifact: criterion agreement confirms consistent application to the same reading of the quantity and does not establish the classification from outside. SCHEMA-FIT FINDING, logged for Architect ruling on the six GENERAL_PRINCIPLES skills: the 11-key contract represented this classification skill WITH STRAIN. formula holds criteria prose rather than an equation and declares a single generic symbol Q; worked_example.answer holds a label set rather than a computed result; failure_signal_mappings is honestly thin at one signal because four of five cannot be earned. No algebra was invented and no signal padded to fill a field.

ordered_steps: Draw or identify the vector and the coordinate axes, including the positive x and y directions.
Identify the angle reference axis and the quadrant in which the vector lies.
Determine which component is adjacent to the given angle and which is opposite (cosine for adjacent, sine for opposite when θ is measured from the reference axis).
Compute the component magnitudes using sine and cosine with the given magnitude and angle.
Assign signs to F_x and F_y based on the vector direction and the axis convention.
Write the vector in component form with units (F = F_x i + F_y j).
Check the result by recomputing the magnitude and verifying the direction sense.

signature.notes: Second Phase D sign-off; worked example independently re-verified 433.0/250.0/approx 500; schema-valid v1_1; canonical-four live mappings; MODULE_INTRO_RENDER_DEFERRED_FRONTEND_TOPIC_FIXTURE_GAP; SOURCE_REFS_DEFERRED_SCHEMA_UNSUPPORTED

ordered_steps: Establish a right-handed xyz frame and state the positive sense of each axis.

Identify the given geometry for the single force: the angle from the reference axis (here, from +z) and the angle of the projection in the stated coordinate plane (here, xy), plus the stated direction sense in each axis.

Project onto the relevant coordinate plane using the out-of-plane angle: assign the plane-projection magnitude and the axis-direction component with sine and cosine correctly for the stated reference (for φ from +z: F_xy = F sin φ and Fz = F cos φ). Do not skip this step and treat one angle as sufficient.
Resolve the in-plane projection into its two rectangular components using the second angle (for θ from +x in the xy-plane: |Fx| = F_xy cos θ and |Fy| = F_xy sin θ).
Assign algebraic signs to Fx, Fy, and Fz from the stated direction of the force relative to +x, +y, and +z.
Write the force in Cartesian form with units: F = Fx i + Fy j + Fz k.

Verify with the magnitude relation F^2 = Fx^2 + Fy^2 + Fz^2, then stop. Do not introduce coordinate direction angles, add other vectors, form position or unit vectors along a line, take a dot or cross product, draw an FBD, or write equilibrium equations.

signature.notes: Batch 4E skill 3/6 — opens the 3D chain. SCOPE WAS OPERATOR-DERIVED, not Architect-ruled: the Batch 4E ruling detailed skill 1/6's scope only. Derived from graph truth and the signed boundaries. The Architect's binding 3D ruling was honored: this is particle-equilibrium debt retirement, not 3D rigid-body expansion — no rigid_body_fbd_3d, no 3D rigid-body equilibrium. Narrow by construction: one force in, three components out. Every adjacent capability is a separate graph node and none appears as an authored step — coordinate direction angles, 3D vector addition, position vectors, unit vectors along a line, dot and cross products, 3D FBDs, and equilibrium are all excluded, and step 7 names them explicitly. ordered_steps: Identify the given 3D Cartesian vectors (components already resolved). Cite cartesian_vector_components_3d for resolving a single vector into components — do not re-derive that resolution here.
Pair like components only: every x with x, every y with y, every z with z. Do not add an x-component to a y- or z-component.
Sum with algebraic signs retained: Rx = Σ (x-components), Ry = Σ (y-components), Rz = Σ (z-components). A negative component subtracts in its axis sum.
Write the resultant as a Cartesian vector: R = Rx i + Ry j + Rz k.

Compute the resultant magnitude R = √(Rx² + Ry² + Rz²). Confirm it differs from the arithmetic sum of the individual magnitudes when the vectors are not collinear and same-sense — component-wise addition is forced.
State the closure check Rx² + Ry² + Rz² = R². Note: a clean swap of which axis receives which resultant component preserves this identity, so the check does not catch an axis swap.

Report R (Cartesian form) and its magnitude with units. Do not extract coordinate direction angles (coordinate_direction_angles), form a position vector from two points (position_vector_3d), or compute a dot or cross product.

signature.notes: Batch 4I skill 1/5. Owns component-wise addition of two or more already-resolved 3D Cartesian vectors: pairing like components, summing with algebraic signs retained, writing the resultant in Cartesian form, computing its magnitude, and stating the closure identity. Boundary: cartesian_vector_components_3d (signed parent) resolves a single vector INTO components and is cited, not re-derived; coordinate_direction_angles owns extracting alpha/beta/gamma FROM a resultant; position_vector_3d owns forming a vector from two points; dot and cross products are separate siblings. Worked example Operator-re-derived from the on-disk prompt: A = -12i -12j -6k N (|A| = 18), B = -6i -2j +3k N (|B| = 7); Rx = -18, Ry = -14, Rz = -3; R = -18i -14j -3k N; |R| = sqrt(324+196+9) = sqrt(529) = 23 N; closure 529 = 23^2. Distinguishing feature bites three ways: the vectors are NOT collinear so component-wise addition cannot be bypassed by scalar reasoning along a line; |A|+|B| = 25 != 23 so adding magnitudes is detectably wrong; and the opposite-sign z pair (Az = -6, Bz = +3) makes the sign-dropping result numerically distinct from both the correct answer and the scalar-addition answer, so the three outcomes are separately routable. The example records the honest limitation that a clean axis swap PRESERVES the closure identity, so the check does not catch a swap - carried from the parent skill's finding rather than overstated. THREE-signal mapping: axis_confusion at step 2 (the like-component pairing step - adding an x into a y or z sum), sign_or_placement_error at step 3 (correct pairing but a lost or flipped sign in the axis sum; a distinct authored act from step 2, not a duplicated crux), unclassified at step 7 (report/boundary - incomplete result, magnitude-only, or reaching into the ceded siblings). solution_sequencing_error OMITTED: the three axis sums are independent and no authored step strands a prerequisite on an out-of-order solve. simple_average_used omitted (Centroids-family). Trig-resolution cross-check N/A recorded affirmatively: components are given already resolved and no inclined vector appears. Three correction lanes preceded sign-off, all Operator-caused and all recorded: CORRECTION-001 replaced a collinear example (B = -2A) that let scalar reasoning bypass the skill; CORRECTION-002 replaced a same-sign example whose sign-drop result reproduced the correct magnitude, so the closure check validated the error the signal targets; CORRECTION-003 removed diagnostic narration that the Operator's own edit spec had introduced into a solution step. Opens Batch 4I.

ordered_steps: Identify the given 3D Cartesian vector A = Ax i + Ay j + Az k with known components. Cite cartesian_vector_components_3d as the inverse skill (angles into components) — do not re-derive a two-angle resolution here. Cite resultant_direction_2d as the 2D analogue.
Compute the magnitude A = √(Ax² + Ay² + Az²).
Assign each component to its own axis angle: cos α = Ax/A with α measured from +x, cos β = Ay/A with β from +y, cos γ = Az/A with γ from +z. Do not swap which component feeds which angle.

Retain each component's algebraic sign in its cosine ratio. A negative component gives a negative cosine and an obtuse angle from that positive axis; a positive component gives an acute angle. Evaluate α = arccos(Ax/A), β = arccos(Ay/A), γ = arccos(Az/A).

Verify the identity cos²α + cos²β + cos²γ = 1. Note: because the identity sums squared cosines, it still closes if the components were assigned to the wrong axes or if a negative sign were dropped — it confirms component–magnitude consistency and does not catch an axis swap or a sign error.
Report all three angles with units (degrees to one decimal place unless the problem specifies otherwise).
Stop at α, β, and γ. Do not add vectors, form a position vector from two points, introduce a unit-vector symbol, or take a dot or cross product.

signature.notes: Batch 4I skill 2/5. Owns extraction of the coordinate direction angles alpha, beta, gamma FROM known Cartesian components: cos alpha = Ax/A, cos beta = Ay/A, cos gamma = Az/A, each angle measured from the POSITIVE sense of its own axis, plus the identity cos^2 alpha + cos^2 beta + cos^2 gamma = 1. Boundary: cartesian_vector_components_3d (signed parent) performs the INVERSE operation, angles into components, cited not re-derived; resultant_direction_2d (signed) is the 2D analogue, one direction angle from planar components with quadrant awareness, and this skill is its 3D extension to three axis-referenced angles; cartesian_vector_addition_3d (signed earlier this batch) forms resultants by addition; position_vector_3d (batch sibling) forms a vector from two points; unit_vector_along_line (downstream, planned) owns the unit-vector deliverable - the artifact notes in one conceptual sentence that the direction cosines ARE the unit-vector components but binds no symbol for it and computes no unit vector; dot and cross products excluded. Worked example Operator-re-derived from the on-disk prompt: A = 2i - 3j + 6k, magnitude sqrt(4+9+36) = sqrt(49) = 7; cos alpha = 2/7 -> alpha = 73.4 deg (acute); cos beta = -3/7 -> beta = 115.4 deg (OBTUSE, from the negative y-component); cos gamma = 6/7 -> gamma = 31.0 deg (acute); identity (4+9+36)/49 = 49/49 = 1. Distinguishing feature bites: the negative y-component produces a genuine obtuse angle against two acute ones, so sign retention has a visible consequence - with no obtuse angle the sign carries none and the skill is not exercised; all three components are nonzero and distinct in magnitude, so no degenerate equal-angle case arises. HONEST LIMITATION recorded in concept, procedure and solution: because the identity sums SQUARED cosines it closes unchanged under a permutation of components among the axes and unchanged if a negative sign is dropped, so it verifies component-magnitude consistency only and catches neither an axis swap nor a sign error - stated as a property of the check rather than overstated, in the same spirit as the parent skill finding and the skill 1 closure note. THREE-signal mapping: axis_confusion at step 3 (the component-to-axis-angle assignment - feeding Ay into cos alpha), sign_or_placement_error at step 4 (correct assignment but a dropped or flipped sign in the cosine ratio, yielding acute where obtuse is required; a distinct authored act from step 3, not a duplicated crux), unclassified at step 7 (report and boundary - incomplete angle set, missing units, treating the identity as catching a swap, or reaching into the ceded siblings). solution_sequencing_error OMITTED: the three angles are computed independently from one magnitude and no authored step strands a prerequisite on an out-of-order solve. simple_average_used omitted (Centroids-family). One correction lane preceded sign-off: CORRECTION-001 moved the identity verification ahead of the report in both the procedure and solution arrays, since a verification that follows the report cannot gate it; strings were moved verbatim with no rewording and no signal retargeting, matching the verify-then-report ordering of cartesian_vector_addition_3d signed earlier in this batch.

ordered_steps: Identify the two points A(xA, yA, zA) and B(xB, yB, zB). Cite cartesian_vector_components_3d for Cartesian form. Do not form a unit vector, a moment, a cross product, a dot product, a projection, a resultant by addition, or direction angles.
For each axis, difference only matching coordinates: x with x, y with y, z with z. Do not subtract across axes or assign a difference to the wrong unit vector.

Apply head-minus-tail in the directed sense FROM A TO B: r_AB = (xB − xA) i + (yB − yA) j + (zB − zA) k. Handle double negatives (subtracting a negative coordinate). State the order relation r_BA = −r_AB.
Compute |r_AB| as the straight-line distance. Do not treat the magnitude as distinguishing order or catching a sign slip — |r_AB| = |r_BA|, and a single flipped component leaves |r| unchanged.

Verify before reporting by reconstructing the head from the tail, component-wise: xA + (xB − xA) = xB, and likewise for y and z. This checks the differencing and its order; it is not a general vector-addition solve.
Report r_AB as a Cartesian vector and |r_AB| as the distance. Do not report a unit vector.
Stop. Do not normalize to a unit vector, compute a moment or cross product, form a dot product or projection, add vectors as a resultant, or extract direction angles.

ordered_steps: Identify the tail point A(xA, yA, zA) and the head point B(xB, yB, zB). State the required direction FROM A TO B. Cite position_vector_3d for the head-minus-tail construction — form r, then normalize; do not re-derive the position vector from first principles. Do not classify the quantity. Do not resolve by a stated angle. Do not scale u to obtain a force vector (force_directed_along_line). Do not form a dot product, a cross product, or a projection.
Assemble the components of r_AB on matching axes only: r_x from the x-coordinates, r_y from the y-coordinates, r_z from the z-coordinates. Do not transpose components between axes.
Form r_AB by head-minus-tail FROM A TO B: r_AB = (xB − xA, yB − yA, zB − zA). Handle subtraction of a negative coordinate. Do not take tail-minus-head.
Compute the magnitude |r_AB| = √(r_x² + r_y² + r_z²).

Normalize: u_AB = r_AB / |r_AB|. State that u_AB is dimensionless and that |u_AB| must equal one. Form the reversed-order result r_BA = −r_AB, |r_BA| = |r_AB|, and u_BA = −u_AB, and record that the order of the points is part of the answer.

Verify before reporting by a route that does not reuse the division: confirm (r_x/|r_AB|)² + (r_y/|r_AB|)² + (r_z/|r_AB|)² = 1, and confirm that metres divided by metres leaves u dimensionless. Record that this check cannot detect a reversed point order or a misread coordinate.
Report u_AB with the stated tail and head (FROM A TO B). Stop. Do not attach units to u, do not scale u to obtain a force vector, and do not form a dot product, a cross product, or a projection.

ordered_steps: Identify each quantity Q to classify. Treat classification as a property of the quantity, not of notation or of whether a stated number carries a sign. Do not classify by the ingredients Q is built from. State the two independent criteria (specification test and combination test). Choose no axes; do not compute components; do not resolve, add, or decompose vectors; do not build a unit vector.
Apply the specification test to each Q: fully specified by magnitude and units alone → SCALAR; additionally requires a direction before it is determined → VECTOR.

Apply the combination test independently to each Q: combine by arithmetic addition of signed magnitudes on a single scale → SCALAR; require head-to-tail composition whose sum depends on the angle between the parts → VECTOR. Do not treat sign cancellation on a line as the vector test.

Confirm that the two criteria agree for each Q. If they disagree, revise the identification of Q or the application of a test. Record that agreement confirms consistent application only — it is not external validation of the classification.
Verify before reporting: re-apply the combination test independently to work and to moment of a force, and confirm each reaches the same classification the specification test already gave.

Report each Q as SCALAR or VECTOR with the stated reason from the criteria. Stop. Do not resolve, add, or decompose vectors; do not choose axes; do not build a unit vector; do not report a bare label without a reason.

ordered_steps: Draw or identify the vector and the coordinate axes, including the positive x and y directions.

Assign signs to F_x and F_y based on the vector direction and the axis convention.

ordered_steps: Establish a right-handed xyz frame and state the positive sense of each axis.

Identify the given geometry for the single force: the angle from the reference axis (here, from +z) and the angle of the projection in the stated coordinate plane (here, xy), plus the stated direction sense in each axis.

Project onto the relevant coordinate plane using the out-of-plane angle: assign the plane-projection magnitude and the axis-direction component with sine and cosine correctly for the stated reference (for φ from +z: F_xy = F sin φ and Fz = F cos φ). Do not skip this step and treat one angle as sufficient.
Resolve the in-plane projection into its two rectangular components using the second angle (for θ from +x in the xy-plane: |Fx| = F_xy cos θ and |Fy| = F_xy sin θ).
Assign algebraic signs to Fx, Fy, and Fz from the stated direction of the force relative to +x, +y, and +z.
Write the force in Cartesian form with units: F = Fx i + Fy j + Fz k.

Verify with the magnitude relation F^2 = Fx^2 + Fy^2 + Fz^2, then stop. Do not introduce coordinate direction angles, add other vectors, form position or unit vectors along a line, take a dot or cross product, draw an FBD, or write equilibrium equations.

ordered_steps: Identify the tail point A(xA, yA, zA) and the head point B(xB, yB, zB). State the required direction FROM A TO B. Cite position_vector_3d for the head-minus-tail construction — form r, then normalize; do not re-derive the position vector from first principles. Do not classify the quantity. Do not resolve by a stated angle. Do not scale u to obtain a force vector (force_directed_along_line). Do not form a dot product, a cross product, or a projection.
Assemble the components of r_AB on matching axes only: r_x from the x-coordinates, r_y from the y-coordinates, r_z from the z-coordinates. Do not transpose components between axes.
Form r_AB by head-minus-tail FROM A TO B: r_AB = (xB − xA, yB − yA, zB − zA). Handle subtraction of a negative coordinate. Do not take tail-minus-head.
Compute the magnitude |r_AB| = √(r_x² + r_y² + r_z²).

Normalize: u_AB = r_AB / |r_AB|. State that u_AB is dimensionless and that |u_AB| must equal one. Form the reversed-order result r_BA = −r_AB, |r_BA| = |r_AB|, and u_BA = −u_AB, and record that the order of the points is part of the answer.

Verify before reporting by a route that does not reuse the division: confirm (r_x/|r_AB|)² + (r_y/|r_AB|)² + (r_z/|r_AB|)² = 1, and confirm that metres divided by metres leaves u dimensionless. Record that this check cannot detect a reversed point order or a misread coordinate.
Report u_AB with the stated tail and head (FROM A TO B). Stop. Do not attach units to u, do not scale u to obtain a force vector, and do not form a dot product, a cross product, or a projection.

ordered_steps: Identify each quantity Q to classify. Treat classification as a property of the quantity, not of notation or of whether a stated number carries a sign. Do not classify by the ingredients Q is built from. State the two independent criteria (specification test and combination test). Choose no axes; do not compute components; do not resolve, add, or decompose vectors; do not build a unit vector.
Apply the specification test to each Q: fully specified by magnitude and units alone → SCALAR; additionally requires a direction before it is determined → VECTOR.

Apply the combination test independently to each Q: combine by arithmetic addition of signed magnitudes on a single scale → SCALAR; require head-to-tail composition whose sum depends on the angle between the parts → VECTOR. Do not treat sign cancellation on a line as the vector test.

Confirm that the two criteria agree for each Q. If they disagree, revise the identification of Q or the application of a test. Record that agreement confirms consistent application only — it is not external validation of the classification.
Verify before reporting: re-apply the combination test independently to work and to moment of a force, and confirm each reaches the same classification the specification test already gave.

Report each Q as SCALAR or VECTOR with the stated reason from the criteria. Stop. Do not resolve, add, or decompose vectors; do not choose axes; do not build a unit vector; do not report a bare label without a reason.

ordered_steps: Establish a right-handed xyz frame and state the positive sense of each axis.

Identify the given geometry for the single force: the angle from the reference axis (here, from +z) and the angle of the projection in the stated coordinate plane (here, xy), plus the stated direction sense in each axis.

Project onto the relevant coordinate plane using the out-of-plane angle: assign the plane-projection magnitude and the axis-direction component with sine and cosine correctly for the stated reference (for φ from +z: F_xy = F sin φ and Fz = F cos φ). Do not skip this step and treat one angle as sufficient.
Resolve the in-plane projection into its two rectangular components using the second angle (for θ from +x in the xy-plane: |Fx| = F_xy cos θ and |Fy| = F_xy sin θ).
Assign algebraic signs to Fx, Fy, and Fz from the stated direction of the force relative to +x, +y, and +z.
Write the force in Cartesian form with units: F = Fx i + Fy j + Fz k.

Verify with the magnitude relation F^2 = Fx^2 + Fy^2 + Fz^2, then stop. Do not introduce coordinate direction angles, add other vectors, form position or unit vectors along a line, take a dot or cross product, draw an FBD, or write equilibrium equations.
