ordered_steps: Identify the given 3D Cartesian vectors (components already resolved). Cite cartesian_vector_components_3d for resolving a single vector into components — do not re-derive that resolution here.
Pair like components only: every x with x, every y with y, every z with z. Do not add an x-component to a y- or z-component.
Sum with algebraic signs retained: Rx = Σ (x-components), Ry = Σ (y-components), Rz = Σ (z-components). A negative component subtracts in its axis sum.
Write the resultant as a Cartesian vector: R = Rx i + Ry j + Rz k.

Compute the resultant magnitude R = √(Rx² + Ry² + Rz²). Confirm it differs from the arithmetic sum of the individual magnitudes when the vectors are not collinear and same-sense — component-wise addition is forced.
State the closure check Rx² + Ry² + Rz² = R². Note: a clean swap of which axis receives which resultant component preserves this identity, so the check does not catch an axis swap.

Report R (Cartesian form) and its magnitude with units. Do not extract coordinate direction angles (coordinate_direction_angles), form a position vector from two points (position_vector_3d), or compute a dot or cross product.

ordered_steps: Identify the given 3D Cartesian vector A = Ax i + Ay j + Az k with known components. Cite cartesian_vector_components_3d as the inverse skill (angles into components) — do not re-derive a two-angle resolution here. Cite resultant_direction_2d as the 2D analogue.

Report all three angles with units (degrees to one decimal place unless the problem specifies otherwise).
Stop at α, β, and γ. Do not add vectors, form a position vector from two points, introduce a unit-vector symbol, or take a dot or cross product.

bindings.micro_skill: Computing centroid of composite areas using weighted averages

ordered_steps: Divide the composite shape into simple sub-shapes (rectangles, circles, triangles).
Identify the reference axis (usually the bottom-left corner or a specified origin).
Calculate the area Aᵢ of each sub-shape.
Locate the centroid (xᵢ, yᵢ) of each sub-shape from the reference axis.
Compute the moment for each sub-shape: Aᵢxᵢ and Aᵢyᵢ.
Sum all moments: ΣAᵢxᵢ and ΣAᵢyᵢ.
Sum all areas: ΣAᵢ.
Divide: x̄ = ΣAᵢxᵢ / ΣAᵢ and ȳ = ΣAᵢyᵢ / ΣAᵢ.

bindings.micro_skill: Building a 2D particle free-body diagram and writing force-balance equations

ordered_steps: Identify the specific particle or point-mass body to isolate (e.g., a ring, pin, knot, or block treated as a particle).
Survey the physical setup and list every external interaction on that body: applied loads, weight, cable/link tensions, normal or contact reactions, and friction if explicitly part of the setup.
Draw the isolated particle as a dot or small symbol at its location, separated from supports and attached members.
For each external force, draw a labeled arrow on the particle at the correct point of application, along the correct line of action, and with the correct sense (direction along that line).
Verify completeness: every contact and field force is shown; no internal forces; no invented forces; each force is named and its line of action is stated.
Confirm the diagram stops at the force inventory — do not resolve forces into x/y components and do not write ΣFx = 0 or ΣFy = 0 (those are downstream skills).

actions: Isolate the particle from its surroundings.

actions: Draw x and y axes.

ordered_steps.title: Establish coordinate axes and sign convention

actions: Write each force in component form.
Use trigonometry for angled forces.
Assign the correct sign to each component.
ordered_steps.reasoning: Equilibrium is applied component by component.
ordered_steps.title: Resolve all forces into x and y components

actions: Write the x-direction equilibrium equation.
Write the y-direction equilibrium equation.
Include every force shown on the FBD.
ordered_steps.reasoning: A particle in equilibrium has zero net force in both coordinate directions.
ordered_steps.title: Apply ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0

actions: Count unknowns and equations.
Solve algebraically for the requested unknowns.
Keep units consistent throughout.
ordered_steps.reasoning: The unknown force magnitudes or angles come from the two equilibrium equations.
ordered_steps.title: Solve the simultaneous equations

actions: Substitute solved values back into both equilibrium equations.
Verify cable tensions are positive if tension-only members were assumed.
Confirm the result matches the geometry of the problem.

ordered_steps.title: Check signs and physical plausibility

bindings.micro_skill: Computing mass moment of inertia for discrete point masses about a fixed axis using I = Σmr²

ordered_steps: State the area-versus-mass contrast prominently: area_moment_of_inertia / area_moment_integral_definition compute I = ∫ r² dA over AREA (dimension L⁴); this skill computes I = ∫ r² dm over MASS (dimension M L²) — same r² structure, different measure and dimension. Do not re-derive the area moment. Name in one sentence that the mass moment of inertia is the quantity that governs resistance to angular acceleration about the stated axis; do NOT author angular acceleration, kinetic energy, stress, or an equation of motion. Cite standard relations as given; do not derive them. The mass parallel-axis relation I = I_cm + m d² is the analogue of the area theorem (transfer A d²); state the analogy and USE the mass form — do not re-derive the area theorem. Exclude product_of_inertia_area, inclined_axis_area_moment, and Mohr's circle. No equilibrium equations.

For each mass element or point mass, form r (or r_i) as the PERPENDICULAR distance to the named axis — not the distance to a point or to the origin, except when the axis through the origin makes those distances coincide. A wrong length that is still a length is a placement error on r.

Select the named axis and the matching expression for r². For discrete point masses at coordinates (x, y): about the z-axis through the origin, r² = x² + y²; about the x-axis, r² = y². Compute I = Σ m_i r_i² for each required axis. Do not mix the r formula of one axis with another. Continuous bodies may also be integrated directly as ∫ r² dm when required.

When an approved standard relation is given for a common shape about a stated axis, substitute and evaluate (for example I_cm = (1/12) m L² for a slender rod about a perpendicular centre-of-mass axis). Transfer to a parallel axis with I = I_cm + m d² when required.

Verify before reporting. (1) Dimensional: every mass-moment result must be kg·m² — a result in m⁴ would signal the area-mass conflation; this check does not catch a wrong length that is still a length. (2) When both a transfer route and an independent tabulated relation are available for the same axis, confirm they agree. Record that each I is only about its stated axis.
Report each mass moment with the named axis and kg·m² units. Stop — do not author dynamics, do not compute an area moment, and do not derive a standard relation presented as given.

bindings.micro_skill: Applying the parallel-axis theorem for second moment of area about parallel axes in 2D

ordered_steps: Identify the single shape, its area A, the named parallel axes, and any I values taken as given. Cite that area_moment_of_inertia supplies centroidal standard results without transferring, and area_moment_integral_definition obtains an axis value by integration without transferring. Do not re-derive those given values and do not integrate. Do not sum multiple shapes.
Identify which of the named axes is the centroidal reference that must anchor I = I_c + A d^2. Do not treat a non-centroidal axis as the reference of the relation.
For each required transfer, determine the perpendicular distance d between the two parallel axes involved and form A d^2.

Apply the theorem in the correct direction: add A d^2 when moving away from the centroidal axis; subtract A d^2 when moving toward it. If neither endpoint is the centroidal axis, transfer through the centroidal axis in two steps. Do not apply the relation directly between two non-centroidal axes.
If a direct transfer between two non-centroidal axes is proposed, reject it and replace it with the two-step route through the centroidal axis.

Verify before reporting. Prefer agreement with an independently obtained value for the same axis when available. Check positivity: transferred values about non-centroidal axes must exceed I_c. Record that positivity catches a direction error but does not catch a wrong-reference direct transfer, and that transferring out and back is circular as a check of the reference choice.
Report each transferred I with the named axis and length^4 units. Stop. Do not integrate, re-derive centroidal standard results, combine shapes, or compute radius of gyration.

bindings.micro_skill: Calculating moment magnitude in 2D

ordered_steps: Identify the moment center O and choose the sign convention (counterclockwise positive, clockwise negative).
Identify the force, either by magnitude and direction or by components F_x and F_y.

bindings.micro_skill: Solving for support reactions using force and moment equilibrium for a coplanar rigid body

ordered_steps: Identify every support or connecting member on the body that supplies a reaction and classify each by type: pin, frictionless roller, fixed (built-in), or cable/two-force link (as present in the setup).
For each classified support, state which rigid-body translations and/or rotations it prevents in 2D.

Map those prevented motions to reaction components using the constraint → reaction principle: one force component per prevented translation direction; one couple-moment reaction if rotation is prevented (fixed supports only among the common 2D types).
Assign a symbol and an assumed positive direction (or clockwise/counterclockwise sense for a couple) to every reaction component in the mapping — do not compute magnitudes.
Label each reaction component on the free-body diagram at the support location with its symbol and assumed sense, matching the mapped set for that support type.

Verify the component count for each support against its type: pin → 2 force components; frictionless roller → 1 force perpendicular to the surface; fixed → 2 force components + 1 couple moment; cable/two-force link → 1 force along the member.

Confirm the deliverable is the support-type → reaction-components mapping only — do not write ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0, or ΣM = 0, and do not solve for any reaction value (those belong to rigid_body_equilibrium_2d and support_reactions_2d).
Identify the rigid body and every support that supplies reactions; classify each support by type (pin, roller, fixed/built-in, cable/link).

Map each support type to its allowed reaction components using the constraint → reaction rule (fixed → two force components plus a couple moment; pin → two force components; roller → one force perpendicular to the surface; cable/link → one force along the member).
Draw the free-body diagram with those reaction components at the supports, assume positive senses, and place all applied loads at their given locations.

Count the independent reaction unknowns. Exactly three unknowns against the three 2D equilibrium equations is the necessary condition to proceed; stop if the count exceeds three (statically indeterminate — not solvable by equilibrium alone). Treat the count as a screening check, not a full determinacy verdict: proper-versus-improper constraint (concurrent or parallel reaction arrangements) belongs to constraints_static_determinacy.
Resolve every inclined applied force into x and y components using the stated axes and angle.
Choose a moment center O that eliminates as many unknown reactions as possible and state why (for a fixed support, O at the wall often removes Ax and Ay from the moment equation).
Write ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0, and ΣM_O = 0, substituting resolved components and including the couple-moment reaction where present.
Solve for every unknown reaction component and couple.
Interpret each signed result: a negative value means the true sense is opposite the assumed positive direction.
Report every support reaction with magnitude, direction or rotational sense, and units.

Confirm a complete 2D rigid-body free-body diagram is already given. List every labeled force and couple and identify the unknown force or moment variables to solve for. Do not remodel support types or invent reaction components that are not already on the FBD.
Establish rectangular axes (+x, +y) and a moment sign convention (state which sense of rotation is positive).
Resolve every inclined force on the FBD into x and y components using the stated axes and the given angle (or given cos/sin).
Count the independent unknowns and confirm they do not exceed the three available equilibrium equations (ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0, ΣM = 0).

bindings.micro_skill: Sketching shear and bending-moment diagrams for a determinate beam with one concentrated load using piecewise values along the span

ordered_steps: Obtain support reactions if they are not given (cite beam_reactions). Do not re-teach the support-type catalog.

Cite the load-shear-moment relations from shear_moment_load_relationships (dV/dx = −w, dM/dx = V, area forms, jump rules, degree rules). State the sign convention. Do not re-derive the relations from first principles.

Construct the complete shear diagram left to right across the whole beam: start just left of the leftmost force, apply a jump at each concentrated reaction or load, apply slope −w under distributed load, and hold V constant on unloaded segments. Record V at every key point (supports, load boundaries, concentrated forces, and where V = 0). Verify closure: V returns to zero after the last vertical reaction.

Only after the shear diagram is fully determined at every key point, construct the moment diagram from the area under V (ΔM = ∫ V dx) and the degree rules. Do not attempt the M diagram before the V diagram exists — without V, the areas that determine ΔM are unavailable. Building M first (or by re-solving ΣM at many cuts instead of using area-under-V) strands that prerequisite.

Construct the complete moment diagram: integrate / accumulate areas under V segment by segment, apply the correct degree (linear V → parabolic M under uniform load), and enforce closure (M = 0 at simple-support or free ends). Record M at every key point, including the station where V = 0.

On the finished diagrams, mark where V = 0 and the M value there as the diagram peak. Do not reframe the deliverable as extracting the numeric global maximum moment alone — that specialization belongs to maximum_moment_from_zero_shear.

Report the complete V and M diagrams by their key-point values and segment shapes/degrees. Stop — do not treat global-max-M extraction as this skill's deliverable, and do not replace traversal with per-point section equilibrium.

bindings.alt_text: dimensional relationship diagram for Computing mass moment of inertia for discrete point masses about a fixed axis using I = Σmr²; authored configuration from curriculum/modules/synthesized/inertia_mass_moment_intro_point_masses_synthesized.json, bound under single procedure.
bindings.micro_skill: Computing mass moment of inertia for discrete point masses about a fixed axis using I = Σmr²

ordered_steps: State the area-versus-mass contrast prominently: area_moment_of_inertia / area_moment_integral_definition compute I = ∫ r² dA over AREA (dimension L⁴); this skill computes I = ∫ r² dm over MASS (dimension M L²) — same r² structure, different measure and dimension. Do not re-derive the area moment. Name in one sentence that the mass moment of inertia is the quantity that governs resistance to angular acceleration about the stated axis; do NOT author angular acceleration, kinetic energy, stress, or an equation of motion. Cite standard relations as given; do not derive them. The mass parallel-axis relation I = I_cm + m d² is the analogue of the area theorem (transfer A d²); state the analogy and USE the mass form — do not re-derive the area theorem. Exclude product_of_inertia_area, inclined_axis_area_moment, and Mohr's circle. No equilibrium equations.

For each mass element or point mass, form r (or r_i) as the PERPENDICULAR distance to the named axis — not the distance to a point or to the origin, except when the axis through the origin makes those distances coincide. A wrong length that is still a length is a placement error on r.

Select the named axis and the matching expression for r². For discrete point masses at coordinates (x, y): about the z-axis through the origin, r² = x² + y²; about the x-axis, r² = y². Compute I = Σ m_i r_i² for each required axis. Do not mix the r formula of one axis with another. Continuous bodies may also be integrated directly as ∫ r² dm when required.

When an approved standard relation is given for a common shape about a stated axis, substitute and evaluate (for example I_cm = (1/12) m L² for a slender rod about a perpendicular centre-of-mass axis). Transfer to a parallel axis with I = I_cm + m d² when required.

Verify before reporting. (1) Dimensional: every mass-moment result must be kg·m² — a result in m⁴ would signal the area-mass conflation; this check does not catch a wrong length that is still a length. (2) When both a transfer route and an independent tabulated relation are available for the same axis, confirm they agree. Record that each I is only about its stated axis.
Report each mass moment with the named axis and kg·m² units. Stop — do not author dynamics, do not compute an area moment, and do not derive a standard relation presented as given.

bindings.micro_skill: Applying the parallel-axis theorem for second moment of area about parallel axes in 2D

ordered_steps: Identify the single shape, its area A, the named parallel axes, and any I values taken as given. Cite that area_moment_of_inertia supplies centroidal standard results without transferring, and area_moment_integral_definition obtains an axis value by integration without transferring. Do not re-derive those given values and do not integrate. Do not sum multiple shapes.
Identify which of the named axes is the centroidal reference that must anchor I = I_c + A d^2. Do not treat a non-centroidal axis as the reference of the relation.

bindings.micro_skill: Solving for support reactions using force and moment equilibrium for a coplanar rigid body

ordered_steps: Identify every support or connecting member on the body that supplies a reaction and classify each by type: pin, frictionless roller, fixed (built-in), or cable/two-force link (as present in the setup).
For each classified support, state which rigid-body translations and/or rotations it prevents in 2D.

Map those prevented motions to reaction components using the constraint → reaction principle: one force component per prevented translation direction; one couple-moment reaction if rotation is prevented (fixed supports only among the common 2D types).
Assign a symbol and an assumed positive direction (or clockwise/counterclockwise sense for a couple) to every reaction component in the mapping — do not compute magnitudes.
Label each reaction component on the free-body diagram at the support location with its symbol and assumed sense, matching the mapped set for that support type.

Verify the component count for each support against its type: pin → 2 force components; frictionless roller → 1 force perpendicular to the surface; fixed → 2 force components + 1 couple moment; cable/two-force link → 1 force along the member.

Confirm the deliverable is the support-type → reaction-components mapping only — do not write ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0, or ΣM = 0, and do not solve for any reaction value (those belong to rigid_body_equilibrium_2d and support_reactions_2d).
Identify the rigid body and every support that supplies reactions; classify each support by type (pin, roller, fixed/built-in, cable/link).

Map each support type to its allowed reaction components using the constraint → reaction rule (fixed → two force components plus a couple moment; pin → two force components; roller → one force perpendicular to the surface; cable/link → one force along the member).
Draw the free-body diagram with those reaction components at the supports, assume positive senses, and place all applied loads at their given locations.

Count the independent reaction unknowns. Exactly three unknowns against the three 2D equilibrium equations is the necessary condition to proceed; stop if the count exceeds three (statically indeterminate — not solvable by equilibrium alone). Treat the count as a screening check, not a full determinacy verdict: proper-versus-improper constraint (concurrent or parallel reaction arrangements) belongs to constraints_static_determinacy.
Resolve every inclined applied force into x and y components using the stated axes and angle.
Choose a moment center O that eliminates as many unknown reactions as possible and state why (for a fixed support, O at the wall often removes Ax and Ay from the moment equation).
Write ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0, and ΣM_O = 0, substituting resolved components and including the couple-moment reaction where present.
Solve for every unknown reaction component and couple.
Interpret each signed result: a negative value means the true sense is opposite the assumed positive direction.
Report every support reaction with magnitude, direction or rotational sense, and units.

Confirm a complete 2D rigid-body free-body diagram is already given. List every labeled force and couple and identify the unknown force or moment variables to solve for. Do not remodel support types or invent reaction components that are not already on the FBD.
Establish rectangular axes (+x, +y) and a moment sign convention (state which sense of rotation is positive).
Resolve every inclined force on the FBD into x and y components using the stated axes and the given angle (or given cos/sin).
Count the independent unknowns and confirm they do not exceed the three available equilibrium equations (ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0, ΣM = 0).
Choose a moment center O and state why it is useful (for example, a point that removes known forces from the moment equation or simplifies arithmetic).
Write the three scalar equilibrium equations ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0, and ΣM_O = 0, substituting resolved components and including every couple with the stated sign convention.
Solve the equation set for the unknown force and/or couple variables.
Interpret each signed result: a negative unknown means the true sense is opposite the assumed positive direction; confirm physical direction against the FBD.
Report each unknown with magnitude, direction or rotational sense, and units. Stop — do not convert the solve into a named-support-reaction beam analysis.
